word:lxx:L700041.explanation: This word is a proper name, preserved as “Abelbaithamaacha” or “Avelvethamaakha.” It identifies a specific named place or person rather than expressing an ordinary action, quality, or idea. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding context.

word:lxx:L700197.explanation: This Greek LXX verb means “slumberless; sleepless.” It describes a person remaining awake rather than sleeping. word:lxx:L700207.explanation: This Greek verb means “compress; press tight”: it describes squeezing or forcing something into a tighter condition. Its precise force in any one passage depends on what is being pressed and the surrounding sentence.

word:lxx:L700342.explanation: Azouba, also rendered Azuva, is a personal name in the Greek Old Testament. It identifies an individual rather than describing an action, quality, or object. word:lxx:L700416.explanation: Aithan, also rendered Ethan, is a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. word:lxx:L700625.explanation: This word refers to an “alabaster box,” a container made from alabaster. It is a noun naming a physical object rather than an action, quality, or person. word:lxx:L700720.explanation: This adverb means “unreasonably”: acting or speaking without a sound basis in reason. word:lxx:L700782.explanation: Amasia is a proper name, referring to a person identified by that name. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in 1 Chronicles 4:34. word:lxx:L700867.explanation: This Greek LXX adjective describes something that is misshapen or unsightly—lacking a pleasing or well-formed appearance. word:lxx:L700885.explanation: This Greek LXX noun means “fisherman” or “angler,” referring to a person who catches fish. word:lxx:L701064.explanation: Anasōzō means to return. It can also describe being rescued.

word:lxx:L701169.explanation: This verb means to relax, loosen, or release what is being held back. It can describe letting something go, easing restraint, or becoming less strict or forceful. word:lxx:L701183.explanation: Annon is a proper name identifying a person in the Greek Old Testament. It is not a word describing an action, quality, or object, but a personal designation. word:lxx:L701213.explanation: This verb means “reflected” or “echoed,” describing something repeated or sent back rather than produced as a wholly new sound or image. word:lxx:L701266.explanation: This Greek LXX verb means “do in return”: it describes responding to someone by carrying out a corresponding action. word:lxx:L701378.explanation: This Greek LXX verb means “renounce”: to openly refuse or give up a person, claim, obligation, or course of action. word:lxx:L701455.explanation: This verb means to lament bitterly—to express deep grief in words or cries. It describes an intense outpouring of sorrow rather than a quiet feeling of sadness. word:lxx:L701521.explanation: This noun means “release” or “deliverance from,” naming freedom from something that restrains, burdens, threatens, or holds a person. word:lxx:L701594.explanation: This Greek LXX verb means “love no more”: it describes the ending or withdrawal of affection toward someone. word:lxx:L703093.explanation: This word is a proper name, rendered “Gērsom” or “Yirsom.” It identifies a person rather than describing an action, quality, object, or relationship. word:lxx:L703170.explanation: This word describes a discharge or a person suffering from gonorrhoea. It is an adjective, so it identifies a condition rather than naming an action. word:lxx:L703361.explanation: This Greek LXX verb means to petition: to make a request or appeal to someone. It describes asking earnestly rather than merely mentioning a desire. word:lxx:L706160.explanation: Thekoum is a place name listed among cities and villages.

word:lxx:L706249.explanation: Thēria (also rendered Thiria) is a proper name in the Greek LXX. word:lxx:L706304.explanation: This Greek LXX verb means “crush”: to press, break, or destroy something with force. It describes an action rather than a person or thing. The word occurs 19 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, appearing across passages translated from several biblical settings. Its exact force—whether physical breaking or the destruction of an opponent—depends on the surrounding verse, but its central idea remains forceful crushing.

word:lxx:L706454.explanation: Iason is a proper name identifying a person, rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It is rendered “Iasōn; Iason” and functions as a personal name in the Greek LXX corpus. This name occurs 15 times, across 15 verses, with most occurrences in 2 Maccabees. Its significance in any particular passage depends on which person named Iason is being discussed there.

word:lxx:L706577.explanation: Iekman is a proper name, rendered “Iekman,” rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in Joshua 19:11. Because the available text does not include the surrounding verse, this cache identifies the name and its normal lexical function but does not determine whether the named referent is a person, place, or other specific entity. Its precise significance in Joshua 19:11 must therefore be read from that verse and its surrounding passage.

word:lxx:L706652.explanation: This word is a proper name rendered “Iesbi” or “Iezvi.” It identifies a named individual or figure rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at 2 Samuel 21:16. The available lexical information gives the name’s recognized renderings but does not provide an additional definition or explain the person’s role. Its precise significance in that passage must therefore be understood from the surrounding verse and narrative context.

word:lxx:L706771.explanation: “Judaic” describes something connected with the Jewish people, their identity, or their religious life. As an adjective, it qualifies a person, practice, object, or matter as belonging to or associated with Judaism. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, this word occurs once, at 2 Maccabees 13:21. Since the surrounding verse text is not available here, the precise thing it describes in that occurrence cannot be stated, but its basic sense remains “Judaic”: relating to the Jewish community or its religious identity.

word:lxx:L706829.explanation: This adjective describes something with an even surface—flat, level, or made equal in height. It can refer to physical ground or another surface that has no significant rise or unevenness. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs three times, all in the deuterocanonical books of 2 and 3 Maccabees. Its central idea remains consistent: a surface or area brought to, or existing at, an even level. The exact force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

word:lxx:L706924.explanation: This word is a personal name, rendered “Iōnadab” or “Ionathav.” It identifies a person rather than expressing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 16 times across 14 verses, including passages in 2 Samuel, 2 Kings, Psalms, and Jeremiah. Because it is a name, its basic meaning is the individual it identifies; the surrounding verse is needed to distinguish which person bearing the name is intended. The name appears in Old Testament narrative and related historical material, but the available information does not provide a further lexical definition.

word:lxx:L707017.explanation: This verb means to confess—to openly acknowledge or admit something. It describes an act of speaking honestly rather than merely holding an opinion inwardly. In the Greek Old Testament, this word appears twice, both times in Exodus 21, so its recorded use is limited to that passage. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding wording and situation, but the central idea remains a spoken confession or acknowledgment.

word:lxx:L707048.explanation: This conjunction means “and actually,” adding a confirming or emphatic point to what has just been said. It joins thoughts while drawing attention to the fact that the next statement is especially true, noteworthy, or contrary to what might have been expected. Its precise force depends on the sentence around it, but its basic function is to connect and reinforce an idea rather than introduce a separate subject. It appears four times in the Greek LXX corpus, all in 4 Maccabees.

word:lxx:L707174.explanation: This word means “burnt offering,” referring to an offering presented to God and burned in worship. It is a noun used in the Greek Old Testament, especially in passages describing Israel’s sacrificial worship. The word occurs 57 times in the Greek Old Testament, with many occurrences in Leviticus and Numbers. Its meaning remains focused on the offering itself rather than on a general gift or sacrifice of any kind.

word:lxx:L707206.explanation: Katabasis means descent, a downward way or slope.

word:lxx:L707273.explanation: This LXX verb means to give something as an inheritance or to parcel it out. It describes the act of assigning or distributing what is to be received as a possession, especially when an inheritance is being allotted. The word occurs twice in the LXX corpus represented here, once in Deuteronomy and once in 1 Maccabees. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea is the deliberate granting or dividing of an inheritance.

word:lxx:L707299.explanation: Slander means harmful or false speech directed against another person. As a noun, it names the act or substance of speaking against someone in a damaging way. This Greek LXX word has one recorded occurrence, in Wisdom 1:11, so its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage. Its basic meaning remains clear: speech that attacks another person’s reputation rather than communicating truth or goodwill.

word:lxx:L707435.explanation: This verb means to “form a counter-party in the state,” describing the action of establishing an opposing party within a state. It is a verb, so it expresses an action rather than a person, place, or object. In the Greek LXX, it occurs once, in Exodus 38:22. The available wording identifies its general lexical sense, while the precise force of the action in that verse belongs to its surrounding context.

word:lxx:L707596.explanation: Keiria means a wrapping or covering.

word:lxx:L707602.explanation: Kendebaios, also rendered Kentheveos, is a proper name identifying a person rather than a general idea or quality. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs five times, all in 1 Maccabees, from 1 Maccabees 15:38 through 16:8. The name itself does not describe an action, virtue, emotion, or spiritual concept; its function is to identify the same named individual wherever it appears. The person’s particular role in any passage must be understood from the surrounding verse and narrative.

word:lxx:L707718.explanation: This noun refers to an omen or to divination—the practice of seeking meaning or guidance through signs. In the Greek Old Testament, the Septuagint, it appears once, in Isaiah 2:6. Its meaning is therefore focused and specific rather than a broad term for every kind of prediction or religious practice. The exact force of the word in Isaiah depends on the surrounding verse and passage, which should be read alongside this basic sense.

word:lxx:L707747.explanation: This Greek LXX noun means a twig or spray—a small branch or leafy offshoot of a plant. It refers to a physical part of vegetation rather than an action or abstract idea. The word occurs three times in the Greek Old Testament and related Wisdom literature, appearing twice in Job and once in Wisdom. Its precise significance in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse and imagery, but its basic sense remains a small branch, sprig, or spray.

word:lxx:L707884.explanation: This Greek LXX verb means “strengthen”: to make someone or something stronger or more firmly established. It describes an action rather than a person, object, or quality. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, at Wisdom 14:16. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not included here, the particular object or situation being strengthened cannot be stated safely. Its central idea remains the giving or receiving of greater strength, stability, or firmness, according to the sentence in which it appears.

word:lxx:L707956.explanation: Kyklothen means circling, or coming from all around.

word:lxx:L708012.explanation: Kōladam, also rendered Kolatham, is a proper name in the Greek Old Testament. It identifies a named person, place, or other entity, but the available lexical information does not specify which kind. This name occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, at Joshua 19:2. Its precise referent is determined by the surrounding verse and passage rather than by the name itself.

word:lxx:L708139.explanation: This Greek LXX verb means “lick up”: to gather or consume something with the tongue. It describes a physical action rather than a person, object, or quality. The word occurs five times in the Greek Old Testament, across four verses, including passages in 1 Kings, Psalms, Isaiah, and Micah. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its basic meaning remains the act of licking something up.

word:lxx:L708221.explanation: This Greek LXX verb means to pray or entreat—to address a plea to God or another person. It describes earnest asking rather than a casual statement. The word appears twice in the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here: once in Psalms and once in 2 Maccabees. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and its subject, but its central idea remains a prayerful or urgent appeal.

word:lxx:L708355.explanation: Madian, also rendered Mathian, is a proper name used in the Greek Old Testament. It identifies a named biblical entity rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. The name occurs 62 times across 57 verses, from Genesis through Habakkuk, with especially frequent use in Judges and additional occurrences in Numbers and Exodus. Its exact reference—whether to a people, territory, or another named subject—depends on the surrounding verse, but the lexical meaning itself is the name “Madian; Mathian.”

word:lxx:L708427.explanation: This noun means an abomination: something viewed as morally or religiously detestable and therefore unacceptable. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears twice, both in Ezra 9, referring to what is condemned as abominable. The word identifies the offending thing itself rather than an action or feeling. Its exact force in either verse depends on the surrounding passage and immediate context.

word:lxx:L708478.explanation: Manthanain is a proper name, used to identify a particular place or named location rather than to express an action, quality, or general idea. It appears twice in the Greek Old Testament, both times in Numbers 21:18–19. The English rendering preserves the name as “Manthanain,” while the lexical record also gives the form “Manthanen.” Without the surrounding verse text, the name itself does not provide further information about the place or its significance.

word:lxx:L708566.explanation: Mastigoō means to scourge or whip.

word:lxx:L708669.explanation: Methla is a proper name preserved in the Greek Septuagint text. It is not presented here as a common word describing an action, quality, or object, but as a personal or place name whose precise referent must be identified from the surrounding passage. The name occurs once in the Greek Old Testament corpus, at Judges 20:48, and is rendered “Methla.”

word:lxx:L708683.explanation: Meinōm is a proper name, identifying a person rather than describing an action, quality, or idea. It is also represented as Minom. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs once, in Nehemiah 7:52. Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, the name’s precise role in that passage cannot be described further. Its basic meaning is therefore its function as a personal name: it distinguishes one individual within the account.

word:lxx:L708764.explanation: Mesollam is a proper name identifying a person rather than a common word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek LXX, it appears twice, both times in 2 Kings: once at 2 Kings 21:19 and once at 2 Kings 22:3. The available wording preserves the name as “Mesollam,” so no broader meaning or translation sense is established here. Its significance in either passage must be understood from the surrounding verse and narrative context.

word:lxx:L708805.explanation: This Greek LXX verb means “regret”: to feel sorrow or dissatisfaction about something previously done, chosen, or experienced. It describes a change of feeling toward an earlier action or decision, rather than merely recognizing what happened. The word occurs 14 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, so its exact force depends on the surrounding passage. As a verb, it expresses what a person does inwardly—regretting something—rather than naming the sorrow itself. Its established meaning is concise: regret.

word:lxx:L708940.explanation: This word means “hire”: to engage someone for work or service. It is a verb, so it describes the act of bringing someone into service rather than naming the worker or the payment itself. In the Greek Old Testament corpus, it occurs 15 times, appearing in passages from Genesis through 1 Maccabees. Its basic sense remains focused on arranging for someone to serve or work. The exact force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

word:lxx:L709015.explanation: Moocha or Mookha is a proper name, functioning as the designation of an individual rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in 1 Chronicles 19:6. The available information identifies the name itself but does not provide enough surrounding verse text to explain the individual’s role or significance in that passage. Its meaning is therefore best understood as a personal name whose particular reference comes from its biblical context.

word:lxx:L709161.explanation: This word means “Nazarite,” referring to a person “consecrated by Nazarite vows.” It is a noun for someone identified by that consecration. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Judges 13:5. The term therefore points to a vow-defined status, not merely to a personal feeling or general devotion. Its precise role in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and verse text.

word:lxx:L709279.explanation: Nephthaleim is a proper name, also rendered Nefthalim. It identifies a named figure or people in the Greek Old Testament rather than describing an action, quality, or object. The name appears 52 times across 48 verses in the Greek Old Testament, from Genesis through Ezekiel. Its precise reference in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but the word itself functions as a name throughout its use.

word:lxx:L709293.explanation: This Greek LXX adjective means “swimming,” describing something associated with swimming or movement through water. It is a descriptive word, not a name for a person, place, or event. In the Greek Septuagint, it occurs once, in Wisdom 19:19. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its basic sense remains connected with swimming and water. word:lxx:L709437.explanation: Oba, also rendered Ova, is a proper personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. word:lxx:L709468.explanation: Ozaza is a proper name preserved in the Greek Old Testament, identifying a particular person or name-bearing figure rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. word:lxx:L709514.explanation: Oikonomos means administrator. An administrator can be charged to carry out a king’s will and that of his company.

word:lxx:L709684.explanation: Ool is a proper name in the Greek Old Testament (LXX), referring to a person named Ool rather than describing an action, quality, or object. It appears once in this LXX corpus, at 1 Chronicles 3:20, and the available rendering preserves the name as “Ool.” Because no verse text or wider passage is included here, the name’s particular family or narrative setting must be understood from that passage, but the lexical meaning supplied is simply the personal name Ool.

word:lxx:L709802.explanation: Hote means when, marking the time or circumstance in which something happens.

word:lxx:L709918.explanation: This noun refers to experience or emotional feeling—the inner response or passion a person undergoes. It can describe what someone feels or passes through, especially when emotion is being considered as a human experience. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs 65 times, with most occurrences in 4 Maccabees. Its precise emphasis in a particular verse depends on the surrounding context.

word:lxx:L709947.explanation: This noun refers to “all the herbage; grass”—the vegetation that covers the ground. It is a general word for plant growth rather than the name of one particular plant. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Job 5:25. That reference identifies its only recorded use, while the word’s basic meaning remains the broad idea of grass or herbage. Its exact force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording.

word:lxx:L710062.explanation: This word refers to the coast or to a place by the sea. As a noun, it can name a coastal area; as an adverb, it can describe location in relation to the sea. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs four times, in Deuteronomy, Judges, Isaiah, and Ezekiel. Its precise force in any one passage depends on the surrounding wording, but its central idea remains a seaside or coastal location.

word:lxx:L710138.explanation: This word is a verb that expresses an action or state. Its basic sense is “point out at the same time”. It describes an action in which something is indicated or brought forward concurrently with something else. The word appears once in the Greek Old Testament, in 2 Maccabees 15:10. Because it occurs only there and no verse text is available here, its precise force in that sentence must be understood from the surrounding passage. Its central idea remains the simultaneous act of pointing something out.

word:lxx:L710167.explanation: Parorgizō means to enrage or provoke.

word:lxx:L710185.explanation: Patassō means to strike or hit.

word:lxx:L710211.explanation: Pedētēs means one who is fettered or a prisoner.

word:lxx:L710336.explanation: Perikompeō means to sound all around.

word:lxx:L710343.explanation: This Greek LXX verb means “leave around”: to leave something remaining or positioned around something else. It describes an action rather than a person, object, or quality. The word occurs four times in the Greek LXX material represented here, appearing twice in 2 Maccabees and twice in 4 Maccabees. Its exact force in any particular sentence depends on what is being left and the surrounding context.

word:lxx:L710400.explanation: This verb means to wall all round—to surround a place with a protective or enclosing wall. It describes the act of enclosing something completely, rather than merely building one section of a wall. In the Greek Old Testament and related LXX corpus, it occurs twice: once in Hosea and once in 1 Maccabees. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse, but its central idea remains clear: creating a complete barrier or enclosure around something.

word:lxx:L710534.explanation: This Greek LXX verb means “make a false note in music”: it describes producing a wrong or discordant note rather than a true one. As a verb, it names an action, not a person or object. The musical image gives the word its central sense—an action that misses the proper note. It occurs 32 times across the Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical books represented here, while its precise force in a verse depends on the surrounding wording.

word:lxx:L710581.explanation: Potheō means to long for or yearn after.

word:lxx:L710659.explanation: This noun means “harm; malignancy,” referring to a damaging or harmful condition, quality, or action. It describes what brings injury or trouble rather than something beneficial or sound. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings, it occurs 69 times, showing a broad use for harm or malignancy across different settings. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains something harmful, damaging, or morally bad in effect.

word:lxx:L710732.explanation: This word means “age.” It is a noun referring to age as a stage or condition of life. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs 14 times, so it is a recurring term rather than a rare expression. Its precise sense in a particular passage depends on the surrounding wording, but its central idea remains age or the condition associated with being advanced in life.

word:lxx:L710790.explanation: This Greek LXX verb means “prepare in advance”: to make something ready beforehand. It describes an action carried out ahead of the time when it will be needed, rather than merely beginning preparation at the last moment. The word appears twice in the Greek Old Testament corpus, once in Isaiah and once in Wisdom. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse, but its central idea remains arranging or making ready beforehand. It is an action word, so it describes what someone does rather than an object or quality.

word:lxx:L710875.explanation: This verb means “give besides”: to provide something in addition to what has already been given. It describes an added gift, payment, or provision rather than the first act of giving. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears three times, in Genesis and Ezekiel. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what is being given and what has already been provided, but its central idea is additional giving or supplying something extra.

word:lxx:L710897.explanation: This verb means “have arrived at,” describing reaching a point, place, or stage. It presents arrival as something already accomplished rather than an action still underway. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs twice, once in 2 Maccabees and once in 4 Maccabees. Its exact force in either passage depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains that something has reached the relevant destination or point.

word:lxx:L710941.explanation: This Greek LXX verb means “shut”: it describes closing something so it is no longer open or accessible. It expresses an action rather than a person, object, or quality. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament represented here, in Genesis 19:6. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning is the act of shutting or closing.

word:lxx:L711050.explanation: This word means “heel,” referring to the rear part of the foot. It is a noun used for that body part in the LXX corpus. The word occurs nine times, including passages in Genesis, Joshua, Judges, and Psalms. Its basic meaning remains concrete and consistent: a heel or the heels. The surrounding verse determines what is being said about the heel in each occurrence.

word:lxx:L711173.explanation: Rhamnon is a proper name preserved as a name rather than translated into an ordinary descriptive word. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in Judges 10:5, and its English rendering is “Rhamnon.” The available information identifies the name but does not provide enough verse text or contextual detail to say whether it refers to a person, place, or something else. Its precise referent must therefore be determined from the surrounding passage.

word:lxx:L711199.explanation: Raphes, also written Rhafes, is a proper name referring to a specific person or place named in the Greek Old Testament. The name itself does not describe an action, quality, or spiritual idea; it identifies someone or something by name. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice: once in 2 Kings 19:12 and once in Isaiah 37:12. Those passages are parallel accounts, but the surrounding verse text is needed to identify precisely what Raphes refers to in each occurrence.

word:lxx:L711317.explanation: “Rōkeim; Rhokim” is a proper name, identifying a named place or designation rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, at Nehemiah 3:8. Because no verse text or surrounding context is available here, the name’s specific historical role cannot be described further. Its ordinary function is simply to identify the named entity mentioned in that passage.

word:lxx:L711418.explanation: Salmana is a proper name, referring to a specific person rather than expressing a general quality, action, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, at Psalms 82:12, and is rendered “Salmana.” The available wording identifies the name but does not provide an additional ordinary meaning or description. Its precise significance in that verse must therefore be understood from the surrounding passage, not from the name alone.

word:lxx:L711447.explanation: “Samaran” is a proper name, used to identify someone rather than to describe an action, quality, or object. Its meaning is simply “Samaran,” with no additional lexical sense supplied. In the Greek Old Testament, this name appears once, in Numbers 26:20. The name itself does not explain the person’s role or significance in that passage; those details belong to the surrounding context. It should therefore be understood as a personal designation, not as a general word with a broader everyday meaning.

word:lxx:L711502.explanation: “Saour” is a proper name, referring to a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, this name appears once, at 1 Chronicles 4:5. It is presented in the available lexical information as “Saour” and “Saur,” two English representations of the same personal name. Because no verse text or wider context is available here, the name itself does not provide a further meaning beyond identifying its bearer.

word:lxx:L711609.explanation: Sebomai means to venerate or stand in awe of, expressed in worship.

word:lxx:L711696.explanation: Seppharim, also called Sepfarim, is a proper name rather than a general word describing an idea or action. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears twice, both times in Isaiah: once in Isaiah 36:19 and again in Isaiah 37:13. Because it is a place or people name in the passage, its identity and significance depend on the surrounding verse and historical setting, not on a broader dictionary sense.

word:lxx:L711735.explanation: This Greek LXX noun means “pen; fold,” referring to an enclosed space used to contain or gather something, especially animals. The central idea is a bounded enclosure rather than an open area. It occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 2 Maccabees 14:33. The word’s precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains an enclosed pen or fold.

word:lxx:L711788.explanation: This Greek LXX noun refers to a cucumber or gourd, a type of produce. It names a food item rather than an action, quality, or person. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Numbers 11:5. The word’s precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its ordinary meaning is the name of this cultivated plant or its fruit.

word:lxx:L711814.explanation: This word means “wheat,” the grain crop used as food. It is a noun naming wheat itself rather than an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 78 times, showing that it is a regularly used term for this important kind of grain. Its appearances range from Genesis through Song of Songs, within both historical and poetic books. The precise significance of wheat in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the word’s basic meaning remains the grain called wheat.

word:lxx:L711937.explanation: Somoron is a proper name, rendered “Somoron” (also “Somorōn”), rather than an ordinary word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX), it occurs five times in four verses. The available lexical information identifies the name but does not provide a further definition or explain its referent; its specific significance in any verse must come from that passage’s surrounding text.

word:lxx:L711968.explanation: Sousakim is a personal name, rendered Susakim for a king of Egypt.

word:lxx:L712037.explanation: This noun means “tenth of a mile,” a unit used to describe distance. It refers to a measured length rather than an action, person, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs eight times, including passages in Daniel, 2 Maccabees, and Susanna. Because the word expresses a specific distance, its precise significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding measurements and events described there.

word:lxx:L712231.explanation: This noun means “mixing together” or “commixture,” referring to the combining of separate things into one mixture. It is a term for the result or process of things being blended together, rather than for one individual object by itself. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Ezekiel 22:19. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea remains a combination formed by mixing things together.

word:lxx:L712284.explanation: This noun means a “juncture” or “seam”—the place where separate parts meet or are joined together. It can describe a joining point, connection, or line of union rather than one of the parts by itself. In the Greek Old Testament, this word occurs once, in Isaiah 41:7. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its basic picture is something joined at a meeting point. It is therefore a concrete term for the connection or seam formed where parts come together.

word:lxx:L712323.explanation: This Greek LXX verb means to place someone beside another person also. It describes bringing or setting one person alongside another, with the added sense that this happens as well. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, in Psalm 93:16. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning centers on positioning someone beside another rather than simply placing something anywhere.

word:lxx:L712356.explanation: The word means “burnt together.” It is a verb describing people or things being consumed by fire as one, with the idea of burning collectively rather than separately. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 6:11. That single occurrence confirms its rarity in this corpus, but the word’s basic meaning remains straightforward: it expresses being burned together. The precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, which is not included here.

word:lxx:L712415.explanation: This noun means a companion at table—someone sharing a meal with another person. It refers to a fellow diner or meal companion, rather than describing the food or the act of eating itself. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in Sirach 9:16. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its ordinary meaning is a person who sits and eats as another’s companion.

word:lxx:L712561.explanation: Systremma means something twisted together. It can describe a body of men. It can also describe a crowd.

word:lxx:L712679.explanation: Sōchōn is a proper name, rendered “Sokhon” in English. It identifies a person named in the Greek Old Testament rather than describing an action, quality, or general idea. This name occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, at 1 Chronicles 4:18. The available wording establishes the name’s identity, but does not provide a separate lexical definition or explain the person’s role in that verse. Its significance therefore comes from the surrounding genealogy and passage context.

word:lxx:L712693.explanation: This adjective describes someone as miserable or suffering—living in a painful, distressed, or pitiable condition. It is a description of a person’s state rather than an action or command. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Isaiah 33:1, so its normal biblical use is represented by that single occurrence. The surrounding verse is needed to explain the specific situation, but the word itself points plainly to misery and suffering.

word:lxx:L712770.explanation: This noun means “completeness” or “accomplishment.” It points to something brought to its intended finish, viewed as complete rather than lacking what is needed. The word appears four times in this Greek Scripture corpus: twice in Judges and twice in Wisdom. Those occurrences show that it can speak of a completed state or achieved result, while the surrounding sentence determines its precise emphasis in each passage.

word:lxx:L712873.explanation: This Greek LXX particle means “actually.” It adds emphasis to a statement, drawing attention to what is true or genuinely the case. Rather than naming a person, object, action, or quality, it modifies the force of nearby words in a sentence. The word occurs eight times in the Greek LXX corpus represented here, all in 4 Maccabees. Its exact emphasis in any particular verse is determined by the surrounding sentence, but its basic function is to underscore or affirm what is being said.

word:lxx:L712950.explanation: This word is a verb that expresses an action or state. Its basic sense is “three times over”. It describes something occurring or being understood in a threefold measure. The word appears once in the Greek Old Testament, in Sirach 43:4. Because the verse text is not included here, its precise force in that sentence must be understood from the surrounding passage. Still, the central idea remains clear: the word marks repetition or degree as threefold, emphasizing that something is done or present three times over.

word:lxx:L713122.explanation: Hyperaspismos means protection—covering with a shield.

word:lxx:L713203.explanation: This verb means “fold over” or “drape over.” It describes placing one thing over another so that it bends, hangs, or covers it. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears twice, both within Exodus 26:12, so its available usage is concentrated in one passage rather than spread widely across the biblical text. As a verb, it expresses an action involving material or an object; the surrounding verse determines exactly what is folded or draped and how the action functions there.

word:lxx:L713276.explanation: This Greek LXX verb means “seize underneath,” describing an action in which something is taken from beneath or by reaching underneath it. It is a verb, so it expresses an action rather than naming a person, object, or quality. The word occurs four times in the Greek Old Testament corpus, in Job, Ecclesiastes, and the Epistle of Jeremiah. Its exact force in any one verse depends on the surrounding passage.

word:lxx:L713351.explanation: This Greek Old Testament noun means “gorge,” referring to a deep, narrow passage or valley in the land. It is a physical geographical term, used for named or recognizable land formations rather than an abstract idea. The word occurs 80 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical material, so it describes a recurring feature of the biblical landscape. Its exact reference in any verse depends on the surrounding place description, but its central meaning remains a gorge or ravine.

word:lxx:L713430.explanation: Phesēchi, also rendered Fesikhi, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a person in the Greek Old Testament and occurs once, in 1 Chronicles 7:33. The available information preserves the name itself but does not provide a separate definition or explanation of its meaning. Its significance in that genealogy comes from identifying the individual named there, while the surrounding verse supplies the specific family context.

word:lxx:L713526.explanation: This noun refers to a blister or pustule, a raised skin lesion. It names a visible bodily condition rather than an action, person, or character trait. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Exodus 9:9–10, and its meaning remains centered on this physical ailment. The word’s precise significance in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its ordinary lexical sense is clear: a blister or pustule affecting the skin.

word:lxx:L713553.explanation: This Greek LXX noun means “litter,” a conveyance used to carry a person. It names the object itself rather than an action or quality. The word occurs three times in the LXX corpus, appearing in 2 Maccabees and Song of Songs. Its precise significance in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse, but its basic meaning remains a litter: a carried seat or vehicle for transporting someone.

word:lxx:L713629.explanation: This verb describes something being “soaked” or “mixed,” especially when material becomes thoroughly saturated or combined. It appears seven times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek biblical books, including passages in Job, Isaiah, Ezekiel, and 3 Maccabees. The surrounding verse determines whether the emphasis is on becoming wet, being blended, or undergoing a similar combining process. Its basic sense concerns material changed through contact with or combination with something else.

word:lxx:L713724.explanation: Charaka means a trench or rampart used in a siege.

word:lxx:L713791.explanation: This adverb means “in a worse way,” describing how an action or situation happens when it is more seriously or badly than another. It focuses on the manner of an action rather than naming a person, object, or event. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 7:39. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its basic sense is a comparison pointing to a more negative manner or condition.

word:lxx:L713852.explanation: This verb means “bereaved,” describing someone who has suffered the loss of a loved one. It focuses on the condition produced by that loss rather than naming the person who died. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs only twice, showing a specific word used in two recorded passages rather than a broad, frequently repeated term. Its occurrences are found in 2 Samuel 13:20 and Jeremiah 28:5. The surrounding verse text is needed to explain the particular situation in either passage.

word:lxx:L713971.explanation: Chryseos means golden or of gold.

word:lxx:L714116.explanation: This LXX verb means “miscarry,” describing a pregnancy that fails to result in birth. It functions as an action word rather than a name or description of a person. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, at Job 21:10, so its normal lexical meaning is clear even though the surrounding verse text is not included here. Its precise force in that passage belongs to the context of the verse and its surrounding statements.

word:lxx:L714163.explanation: This word means “just as” and functions as an adverb that compares one statement, action, or circumstance with another. It introduces a likeness or correspondence, helping connect ideas by showing that something happens in the same way as something else. It appears 259 times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented in this corpus, so it is a common word for drawing comparisons. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence.
